raw_case_text: A 26-year-old male presented with documented fever, anorexia with mild nausea for 20 days. Fever work-ups including malarial antigen test, dengue, typhus, Widal test, and urine routine microscopy were done outside, and all were negative. At admission, vitals were stable, hemogram revealed a leucocyte count of 6700/muL, with normal hemoglobin and platelets. Elevated value of ESR was 68/hr and CRP (18 mg/dL). Chest X-ray was normal. Ultrasound abdomen showed minimum free fluid in the abdomen, ileal thickening for a segment 6 cm of size 9 mm, with few mesenteric lymph nodes. Computed tomography abdomen confirmed the ultrasound findings (Fig. 4). Blood culture revealed S. typhi growth on the third day of admission. Ceftriaxone was given but the fever didn't respond by the 7th day when the patient underwent colonoscopy. Meanwhile, the IGRA test was positive and tuberculosis suspicion arose. On colonoscopy, ascending colon and caecum showed few superficial ulcers maximum size 5-6 mm with surrounding erythema seen. The ileocecal valve and ileum to 12 cm displayed edematous mucosa with superficial ulcers, ileum was less distensible. Beyond 12 cm transition to normal mucosa is seen. Ileum is seen till 30 cm. A few more superficial ulcers maximum 8 mm in size were seen around 20 cm while the rest of the mucosa was normal (Fig. 5). Biopsy from ileocecum showed preserved architecture with marked surface ulceration with dense and diffuse lymphohistiocytic admixed with neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate. No acid-fast bacilli or fungal organisms were identified on special stains. Gene Xpert test was negative. Fever responded to the 12th day of antibiotics and the course was given for five more days. At the 6-month follow-up review CT scan showed normal ileum and no lymphadenopathy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male presented with a 20-day history of documented fever, anorexia, and mild nausea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced 20 days of documented fever accompanied by anorexia and mild nausea. Prior outpatient fever evaluations—including malarial antigen testing, dengue serology, typhus workup, Widal test, and routine urine microscopy—were all negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, anorexia, and mild nausea.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were stable on admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Outpatient malarial antigen, dengue, typhus, Widal test, and routine urine microscopy were negative. Admission hemogram showed a leukocyte count of 6,700/µL with normal hemoglobin and platelet counts. Inflammatory markers were elevated with ESR 68 mm/hr and CRP 18 mg/dL. Chest X-ray was normal. Abdominal ultrasound revealed minimal free intraperitoneal fluid, ileal thickening (9 mm wall thickness over a 6 cm segment), and a few enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) for tuberculosis was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan confirmed minimal free fluid, segmental ileal thickening, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Colonoscopy on day 7 showed a few superficial ulcers (maximum 5-6 mm) with surrounding erythema in the ascending colon and cecum, edematous and less distensible mucosa with superficial ulcers involving the ileocecal valve and terminal ileum up to 12 cm, normal transition beyond 12 cm, and additional superficial ulcers (up to 8 mm) around 20 cm (visualized up to 30 cm). Ileocecal biopsy demonstrated preserved crypt architecture with marked surface ulceration and a dense, diffuse lymphohistiocytic infiltrate admixed with neutrophils; special stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi as well as Mycobacterium tuberculosis GeneXpert were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Typhoid fever with ileocecal ulceration, confirmed by blood culture yielding Salmonella typhi on day 3 of admission and characteristic lymphohistiocytic ulcer histopathology. Intestinal tuberculosis (suspected due to positive IGRA and ileal thickening), fungal enteritis, malaria, dengue, and typhus were ruled out. Intravenous ceftriaxone was initiated; fever persisted past day 7 but resolved on day 12 of antibiotic therapy, which was continued for 5 additional days. At 6-month follow-up, repeat abdominal CT demonstrated a normal ileum and complete resolution of mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
